div.head: FINANCE OF THE CHESTER DIOCESE.
div.p: THE FINANCE OF THE CHESTER DIOCESE.

The money troubles of the diocese of Chester, must be very discouraging to good Churchmen. The annual meeting of the Cuester Diocesan Finance Association wall held at Altriuoham, on Saturday, under the presidency of the Die icip of Chester. The report regretted the madequate support which had been accorded to the various ob- ject. for which the association is working. One speaker remarked that in the diocese of Chester there were 112 livings, the income of which did not amount to £2OO a year, and 11 in which the income did not exceed £5O. Bearing in mind the luxuries that some of them enjoyed, His Lordship thought it was surprising in what a wretched and miserable condition the clergy wore allowed to remain. Some of them were suffering from the most abject poverty, and that being so, could not possibly be fit to carry en their work with any degree of vigour or success, A. very largo sum was required to raise the benefices to anything like an 'Adequate in- come, and yet the receipts were actually falling off. Really, these humiliating and lachrymose declarations made respecting one of the richest dioceses of the English Church are almost calculated to persuade the public that the disendowment and disestablishment of the Church and a direct appeal made to the generosity,—nay, the honest liberality,— of its own wealthy congregations, would not be a calamity, without very great, indeed, ' inoalculable compensations.

Midhat Peelle the Primo Minister, who thought to neutralise the Conference by a paper Constitution for Turkey, has mysteriously disappeared from the scene, and is at this moment an exile on one of the Isles of Greece. It would be idle to specu- late on the cameos of an event which puzzles the high politicians of Europe. The con- jecture is hazarded by correspondent' on the spot that the fall of the Minister remove. i the greatest obstacle to Peace, and that it is I not now improbable that Turkey may make the opportunity of arranging with the Powers and making concessions beneficial to I the Christians. It is likely that the earliest discussions on Eastern affairs, which will , take place in the English Parliament will throw a flood of unexpected light on that hitherto unanswerable Eastern Question. Lord Besoonsfield's Ministry will need all the dexterious subtlety of its thief to recon- cile his own Guild-hall and other declare. dons with the proceedings and policy of his own envoy, Lord Oaliebury. In another week or two much will probably be revealed.
